thread.title: Measles Exposure Alert at LAX: Traveler Arrives on Cathay Pacific Flight
thread.title_full: Measles Exposure Alert at LAX: Traveler Arrives on Cathay Pacific Flight

author: CBSLA
title: Measles Exposure Alert at LAX: Traveler Arrives on Cathay Pacific Flight
text:
Los Angeles County health officials warn of potential measles exposure after an infected traveler arrived at LAX on Cathay Pacific flight CX884 from Hong Kong on June 11, 2026. Exposure locations include the airport shuttle and a hotel; vaccination is urged.
Public health officials in Los Angeles County have issued a measles exposure alert after a traveler with a confirmed case of the disease arrived at Los Angeles International Airport ( LAX ) on June 11, 2026.
The individual traveled on Cathay Pacific Airlines flight CX884, which departed from Hong Kong International Airport and landed at LAX's Tom Bradley International Terminal at approximately 10:45 a.m., according to flight-tracking data from FlightAware. The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health is collaborating with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to identify and notify passengers who were seated near the infected traveler during the 12-hour flight.
Measles is a highly contagious viral illness that can spread through coughing, sneezing, or even being in the same room as an infected person. Symptoms typically appear 7 to 21 days after exposure and include high fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and a characteristic rash that starts on the face and spreads to the rest of the body.
The health department has urged anyone who may have been exposed to monitor for symptoms until July 2, 2026, which is 21 days after the potential exposure. Those who have not developed symptoms by that date are no longer considered at risk. The MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine is highly effective, with two doses providing 97% protection and one dose offering 93% protection.
Unvaccinated individuals are at the highest risk of contracting the disease and developing severe complications, including pneumonia, encephalitis, and even death. The health department has also identified specific locations where people may have been exposed. On June 11, between 10:45 a.m. and 11:45 a.m., the traveler rode the Hilton Los Angeles Airport Hotel Shuttle from the Tom Bradley International Terminal to the hotel.
Subsequently, from 11:15 a.m. to 12:15 p.m., they were present at the Hilton Los Angeles Airport Hotel located at 5711 W Century Blvd. , Los Angeles, CA 90045.
Additionally, the traveler visited several healthcare facilities, which are in the process of notifying potentially exposed patients and staff. The health department has advised anyone who develops symptoms to call their healthcare provider before visiting a medical facility and to inform them of the potential exposure to prevent further transmission. This incident comes amid a surge in measles cases both domestically and internationally.
As of June 12, 2026, the United States has reported 2,073 measles cases this year, with the majority occurring among unvaccinated individuals or those with unknown vaccination status. Approximately 6% of cases have required hospitalization. The outbreak has been particularly severe in Mexico, where more than 18,300 cases have been reported so far in 2026. The Los Angeles County Health Department has cautioned residents traveling to Mexico to exercise increased vigilance and ensure they are fully vaccinated before departure.
Local counties, including San Bernardino, have also reported measles cases, with San Bernardino noting its first case since 2023. Health officials are emphasizing the importance of vaccination as the most effective defense against measles. Dr. Muntu Davis, Los Angeles County Health Officer, stated, 'As measles cases increase, it is important that residents take steps to make sure they are fully protected.
The MMR vaccine is the safest and most reliable way to prevent measles and protect yourself, your family, and your community.
' The health department continues to urge all residents to check their vaccination records and consult with healthcare providers if they are unsure of their immunization status. Measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, but recent outbreaks linked to international travel and declining vaccination rates have led to a resurgence of the disease.
Public health authorities stress that maintaining high vaccination coverage is critical to preventing outbreaks and protecting vulnerable populations, such as infants too young to be vaccinated and individuals with compromised immune systems. The situation remains under investigation, and further updates will be provided as more information becomes available
